Estimating prevalence

Source: vignettes/articles/tutorial-prevalence.Rmd
tutorial-prevalence.Rmd
library(MMSpower)

A national malaria programme wants to know how common a drug-resistance marker (say, a validated kelch13 mutation) is in one region. Earlier reports suggest about 20% of infections carry it, and the programme wants to estimate the prevalence to within ±5 percentage points, with 95% confidence.

Two functions do the work: design_precision() says how many samples to collect, and estimate_prevalence() analyses them once they are in.

Part 1: Designing the study

How many samples, ignoring clustering?

Start with the simplest case: every sample is independent (as if drawn by simple random sampling across the region) and the test is perfect.

d0 <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05)
d0
#> $n
#> [1] 246
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 246

So 246 samples are needed. This is the familiar z2p(1−p)/MOE2z^2 p(1-p) / \text{MOE}^2 formula, rounded up. Two things drive it: the margin of error (halving it roughly quadruples the sample size) and the expected prevalence (the sample size is largest at 50%). If the expected prevalence is uncertain, using a value closer to 50% is the cautious choice.

An imperfect test

Molecular assays are good but not perfect. Suppose the assay has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%: it misses some true positives, and some negatives are wrongly called positive.

d_test <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05,
                           sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
d_test$n
#> [1] 365

The sample size rises from 246 to 365. The reason is that the analysis will correct the measured prevalence back to the true scale (the Rogan-Gladen correction), and this correction stretches the confidence interval by a factor of 1/(Se+Sp−1)1 / (Se + Sp - 1). To keep the same margin of error on the true scale, more samples are needed. Specificity matters more than its size suggests: at low prevalence, false positives can make up a large share of the positives.

Clustering: samples come from sites

In practice samples are collected at a number of sites (health facilities, villages), not drawn at random from the whole region. People at the same site tend to be more alike than people at different sites, so each extra sample from a site adds less information than a sample from a new site. The intra-cluster correlation (ICC) measures how strong this is, and the design effect Deff=1+(npersite−1)ICCD_{eff} = 1 + (n_{per\,site} - 1)\,\text{ICC} says how much the sample size has to grow. For this tutorial we assume an ICC of 0.05, and go back to a perfect test to keep the numbers simple.

There are two ways to fix the design, depending on what is constrained in the field.

Fixing people per site. If each site can realistically collect 20 samples, solve for the number of sites:

d_per <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_per
#> $n
#> [1] 480
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 24
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 20
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.95
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 246

The study needs 24 sites of 20 people, 480 samples in total.

Fixing the number of sites. If the programme already has 20 sentinel sites, solve for the number of people per site:

d_sites <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_sites
#> $n
#> [1] 620
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 20
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 31
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 2.5
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 246

Each of the 20 sites now needs 31 people, 620 samples in total.

In both cases n_eff is the unclustered answer from the first section: the clustered design carries the same information as 246 independent samples. Fixing the sites at 20 needs more samples in total than fixing 20 people per site, because the people per site go up, and so does the design effect.

Too few sites. With the number of sites fixed, there is a limit. Each site is worth at most 1/ICC1 / \text{ICC} independent samples, however many people are tested there, so a small number of sites can never reach the target precision:

design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 10, icc = 0.05)
#> Error:
#> ! Target MOE of 5.0% is unachievable with 10 sites and ICC = 0.050; the minimum achievable MOE is 5.5%.

The error reports the best margin of error that 10 sites can give. The options are to add sites, accept a wider margin of error, or (if there is evidence for it) assume a smaller ICC.

More sites, fewer samples

The same precision can be reached with many different numbers of sites, and spreading the samples over more sites reduces the total needed:

sites <- c(15, 20, 30, 50, 100)
total <- sapply(sites, function(k)
  design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = k, icc = 0.05)$n)
data.frame(sites, per_site = total / sites, total)
#>   sites per_site total
#> 1    15       87  1305
#> 2    20       31   620
#> 3    30       14   420
#> 4    50        7   350
#> 5   100        3   300

With 15 sites the study needs 1305 samples; with 100 sites, only 300, close to the 246 an unclustered survey would need. Each new site brings in fresh information, whereas each extra sample at a site partly repeats what that site has already shown. So, where the budget and logistics allow, aim for more sites with fewer people at each. Site visits cost money too, and the Costing a study tutorial shows how to find the cheapest design.

Part 2: Analysing the data

Suppose the programme settles on 20 sites of about 30 people, and records the number of samples carrying the marker (x) and the number tested (n) at each site:

x <- c(4, 9, 6, 2, 11, 7, 5, 8, 3, 6, 10, 4, 7, 5, 12, 6, 3, 8, 5, 7)
n <- c(30, 32, 28, 31, 30, 29, 33, 30, 27, 31, 30, 32, 29, 30, 31, 28, 30, 30, 32, 29)

The estimate

By default the ICC is estimated from the spread of the site prevalences, and an exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval is returned:

est <- estimate_prevalence(x, n)
est
#> $prevalence
#> [1] 0.2126246
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.172139
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.2577502
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.04280562
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 424.3709
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0.01434799
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.41857
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] 19

The estimated prevalence is 21.3%, with a 95% interval from 17.2% to 25.8%. deff is the design effect worked out from the estimated ICC, and n_eff is the number of independent samples the clustered data are worth. df is the number of sites minus one: the ICC was estimated from 20 sites, and the interval is widened a little to allow for the uncertainty in that estimate (see below).

Choosing an interval method

Three interval methods are available. They give the same point estimate but different intervals:

cp <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "clopper-pearson")
c(cp$ci_lower, cp$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1721390 0.2577502

wald <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "wald")
c(wald$ci_lower, wald$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1710528 0.2541964

ac <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "agresti-coull")
c(ac$ci_lower, ac$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1739951 0.2571266

With this much data and a prevalence well away from 0 they are close. The differences matter for small samples or a prevalence near 0 or 1. There the Wald interval is too narrow, has zero width when no positives are seen, and its limits can fall below 0 or above 1. estimate_prevalence() cuts such limits back to 0 or 1, but that hides the problem rather than fixing it. Clopper-Pearson, the default, is the cautious choice, and Agresti-Coull a good compromise. design_precision() sizes a study with the simpler Wald formula, so a Clopper-Pearson interval usually comes out a little wider than the margin of error the study was designed for. See ?estimate_prevalence for the details.

Supplied or estimated ICC?

The interval depends on the ICC, and estimating an ICC needs data from many sites: with only a handful, the estimate is unreliable. estimate_prevalence() allows for this by widening the interval according to the number of sites the ICC was estimated from. With many sites this makes little difference, but with a handful the interval becomes very wide. So with few sites it is often better to supply a cautious value, for example from earlier surveys in similar settings:

est_icc <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, icc = 0.05)
c(est_icc$ci_lower, est_icc$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1630936 0.2692575

With 20 sites the estimate is usable: it gave an ICC of 0.014 and an interval from 17.2% to 25.8%, while supplying 0.05 gives 16.3% to 26.9%. The clustering concepts article shows how variable ICC estimates are with few sites.

An imperfect test at analysis

If the assay is imperfect, give its sensitivity and specificity, and the estimate and interval are corrected to the true-prevalence scale:

est_test <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
c(est_test$prevalence, est_test$ci_lower, est_test$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1913230 0.1436929 0.2444121

The corrected prevalence is lower than the measured one, because at this prevalence false positives outnumber missed cases, and the interval is wider. The sensitivity and specificity given here should be the same values assumed when the study was designed: the design only delivers the planned margin of error if the analysis makes the same correction.
